Then I stack the large dataset with its covariates and responses and the small data set without responses but with its covariates.

Error in (function (data, A, effects, tag = "", compress = TRUE, remove.unused = TRUE)  :

  Row count mismatch for A: 423,305

                             prior.sigma=c(1, 0.01)) ### P(sigma>1)=0.01
pcprec <- list(prior = 'pcprec', param = c(1, 0.01)) #prior PC-PRIOR de Simpson et al. 2017 Simpson, D. P., H. Rue, A. Riebler, T. G. Martins, and S. H. Sørbye. 2017. “Penalising Model Component Complexity: A Principled, Practical Approach to Constructing Priors.” Statistical Science 32 (1): 1–28.

for (i in 1:length(BIPOS)){

    data=list(y=NA),

    scale.model = TRUE, # scaling this random effect

messages.body_plain:
Hi,

Can you check the actual number of rows in the variables given to the failing inla.stack call?  Since you supply (A,1) for the A matrices, it tries to infer the required size of the second A matrix, and apparently that doesn’t match your other inputs, either the effect or response variable.

Also, even though the error occurs in inla.stack, are you supplying the needed 2 column matrix input needed for a 2-likelihood model?

You say the error happens when you run INLA(), but the error looks like it comes from inla.stack(). Can you supply the output from
  traceback()
when run after the error message appears?

Finn

Finn

messages.subject: Binomial model with offset
messages.subject_clean: Binomial model with offset
messages.body_plain:
Hello list,

I am modelling my data with a binomial outcome:

yi,j ∼ Bin(pi,j , ni,j )
logit(pi,j ) = Xi,j + β + zi,j

where n is the number of success and p the number of trials.

Now, both n and p in my dataset are recorded at non constant intervals, and I suspect that the proportion of success is somewhat related with the exposure time.
I'd therefore like to add an offset term in my model, however I am not quite sure how the offset term would interact with the trials in the left hand side of the binomial likelihood in INLA.

Can anyone explain this to me?

Thanks

That's a singular matrix. For example, the row and column sums are zero.
To answer how one can get around that we’d need to know more about what you’re actually trying to compute; there are usually other ways of calculating quantities involving singular precision matrices, that doesn’t require inverting the singular matrix itself.

Finn

messages.body_plain:
you can add an offset using

	y ~ ... + offset(var) + ...

and then 'var' will be added as a constant in the formula.

about the second question: have you considered to view y_ij as Poisson
instead?  then the expose time is just there in the mean, see 'E' in
the poisson definition.

H

messages.subject: Latent marginal predicted values from INLA GLMM?
messages.subject_clean: Latent marginal predicted values from INLA GLMM?
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

I am wondering whether it is possible in INLA to obtain marginal predicted values (computed using only fixed effects) for original data on the latent scale?

A little background to clarify my problem:
I am currently running animal models in R INLA to do variance component analysis. However I would like to get the variance estimates on the data scale rather than the latent model scale (more biologically interesting) and am using a convenient package "QGglmm" to do this (see attached paper and how to PDF). On page 22-23 of the "how to use QGglmm" PDF you will see that, when fixed effects are included in a model, the package requires "yhat": marginal predicted values from the INLA model (computed using only fixed effects), and the predictions must be computed on the latent scale. As comparison, in an MCMCglmm model output the predict(model, type="terms") function would allow me to get these values.

Currently I have used "control.compute=list(dic=T,config = TRUE)" when running my INLA models, and obtained the predicted values for my original data (i.e. not including NAs in the response phenotype) using "Data$summary.fitted.values". Then I transform these values to the latent scale using the link function (logit link for my binary models, log link for my zero inflated negative binomial model).

I am wondering if random effects affect these fitted values ("predictions"), or whether they are computed using only fixed effects. I also wonder if it is correct to use the log link to transform fitted values to the latent model scale for the "zeroinflatednbinomial1" family.

Thanks in advance,

Sarah Lundregan
NTNU Trondheim, Norway

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Latent marginal predicted values from INLA GLMM?
messages.subject_clean: [r-inla] Latent marginal predicted values from INLA GLMM?
messages.body_plain:
the predictions from the fitted values are computed from the linear
predictor using like exp(linear.predictor), if the link function is the
'log'  (and the appropriate flag is given to do so, link=...)

If the linear predictor contains random effects, then those are
included in the fitted values. Often, is the random effects are of the
'classical style', like model="iid", then their mean is zero so the
predictions with and without the random effects will mostly differ in
the variance (although E(exp(...))  depends also on the variance of
...).

You can easily compute the predictions only using the fixed effect if
you want to, either by using posterior samples, as you mention, or
using linear combinations (see the FAQ page).

If you want to predict the outcome of the zeroinflated output, then its
much easier to stay with the posterior sample stuff. (see also
inla.posterior.sample.eval()  which simplify life...)

Best
H

I have more than 4 levels, but I assume that shouldn't be a problem other than having to write a bit more? I'd prefer to not use shrinkage if possible.

Thanks again!

/Erik

Den tisdag 30 april 2019 kl. 13:41:18 UTC+2 skrev Haakon Bakka:

> Hi,
>
> I suggest just using a manual intercept, then you know what is going on. There are ways to check what you are doing when you make automatic choices, but it is unneccesarily intricate compared to just defining your choices manually.
>
> With factors, what I prefer to do is
> 1. for small factors, define the 0-1 equivalents manually myself
> 2. for larger factors (4+ levels) define an iid effect over the factor levels
>
> For your problme, think about the manual intercept as the "baseline" for the factor. Then all the factor levels describe a change from this baseline. If you do not specify a random effect shrinkage (iid effect), or remove one factor level, your model does not make any sense.
>
> How the defaults for factors and intercept combinations interact with stack is unknown to me, so I suggest setting it up manually and not relying on automatic expansions when using stack.
>
> Best,
> Haakon
>
>
>

Is there any way to check if it actually is applied more than once? And if it is, is there any way to prevent it? I've to add to Haakon's excellent advice and warn that the intercept is the bias of the random error and acts as the first moment of the model and thus removing it needs mathematical support. Removing it creates biased errors (even without space-time or other row based bias). I believe completeness, sufficiency, efficiency etc gets affected too ... Rudy

messages.body_plain:
Thanks for your email and comment.

In my view, it is more that in the simple model

	y ~ 1 + x

then the intercept do what its supposed to do.

with the 'A' matrix, there the data depends on the linear predictor
eta*, where

	eta* = A %*% eta

and eta is defined through the formula

	y ~ 1 + x

then the intercept appears as an intercept in 'eta' and not as an
intercept in the 'eta*'. In most cases, this is not what the user want,
so this is why it is recommended not to use the '1' in the formula (ie
use '-1' instead), but define explicitely what you want.

H

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Hierarchical model including diagnostic uncertainty
messages.subject_clean: [r-inla] Hierarchical model including diagnostic uncertainty
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

let me write that in (hopefully) more precise mathematical notation,
to make sure I understand what you mean.
Some notation:
- \phi, the density function of a standard N(0,1) variable.
- z, a known (or measured) value for a specific individual
- \pi, u_1, u_2, s_1, s_2, unknown parameters, to be estimated.
- prob(z), the probability (or rather conditional probability) an

identified individual is infection positive

prob(z) = \pi \phi[(z-u_1) / s_1] / s_1 / \{ \pi \phi[(z-u_1) / s_1] /
s_1 + (1-\pi) \phi[(z-u_2) / s_2] / s_2 \}

There's a practical difference here if z is a property of the
individual, or if it's a property of a _potential_ individual with
certain characteristics.
Example from ecology:
- the size of a group of dolphins in a property of each specific group
- the roughness of the sea is a property of the ocean in which the dolphins live
Both affect detectability of groups. However, one cannot have group
size without a group, but the state of the
sea at a certain potential group location doesn't care if there is a
group there or not.

In the group size case one needs to model the distribution of group
sizes (possibly with space dependent parameters) explicitly, since one
needs to know what characteristics a specific group that was or
_wasn't_ observed might have.
In the sea state case, one just needs to extend the model into
time-dependent detectability.

I don't quite see how your problem would motivate using the above
probability as a thinning probability for a Poisson process, or what
"z" is, and what the domain of the point process would be. However,
assuming that is what you need, in inlabru you could define a model
with predictor
  \eta(s,z) = \log \lambda(s) + \log prob(z)

You would need \pi, u_!, u_2, and s_1, and s_2 to be defined as
transformation of latent gaussian variables, e.g.
\pi = inverselogit(w_1)
u_1 = w_2
u_2 = w_3
s_1 = exp(w_4)
s_2 = exp(w_5)
where each w is a N(0,1) "iid" latent gaussian variable.

The resulting nonlinear model in the w-parameters is linearised iteratively.
In this case, the resulting prob(z) model doesn't look very appealing
to estimate, as it will be hard to identify the parameters, so I'm not
sure how practical this particular approach would be.

Finn

Dear all,

I recently ran into the following problem when I tried to run some inla models for spatial data.

I have two latent components s1 and s2 with alpha fixed to 3/2, and their parameter estimates (median) are:

s1 range = 1633, s2 range = 530
s1 sd = 0.18, s2 sd = 0.51
my spatial domain is about 50000 by 50000.

The two problems:

sd(mod$summary.random$s1$`0.5quant`) = 0.08
sd(mod$summary.random$s2$`0.5quant`) = 0.03

-- while I don't expect they should match the hyperparameter estimates, I don't know why the sd of s2 median estimates at mesh points are smaller than s1

pred.loc <- spsample(mydomain, 5000, type = "random")
preds <- inla.mesh.project(inla.mesh.projector(mesh.point, loc = pred.loc@coords), mod$summary.random$s1$`0.5quant`) # project to random locations
pred.w1 <- SpatialPointsDataFrame(pred.loc, data.frame(w1 = preds))
plot(variogram(w1~1, pred.w1, cutoff = 10000)) # calculates sample variogram values

messages.subject: INLA behavior with categorical variable
messages.subject_clean: INLA behavior with categorical variable
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I am having some issues with fitting a model with one (or several) categorical variables in a logistic regression model. My understanding based on looking at a number of examples was that INLA would fit factors relative to one of the levels. I am not getting that behavior - I get a fit to each level separately and I can't figure out why this is happening and more importantly how to interpret the values I am reading.

For a quick example, this is how a toy model is specified (the actual model has a random effect and a bunch of other fixed effects):

formula <- Y ~ -1 + intercept + TESTFAC

result_mod <- inla(formula_mod,
                       family = "binomial",
                       data = data_run_inla,
                       Ntrials = N_rep,
                       control.fixed = list(mean = 0, prec = 1/100),
                       verbose = TRUE,
                       keep = FALSE, debug = TRUE)

summary(result_mod) returns this:

> Fixed effects:
>                 mean     sd 0.025quant 0.5quant 0.975quant    mode kld
> intercept     0.6565 5.7735   -10.6789   0.6563    11.9824  0.6565   0
> TESTFACGREEN  0.8114 5.7735   -10.5239   0.8112    12.1373  0.8114   0
> TESTFACRED   -0.1549 5.7735   -11.4903  -0.1551    11.1710 -0.1549   0

Just so it's clear, the "TESTFAC" variable is indeed a factor and has only 2 levels:
 > class(data_run_inla$TESTFAC)
[1] "factor"
> levels(data_run_inla$TESTFAC)
[1] "GREEN" "RED"

In addition, the data doesn't have NAs, and the 'Y' variable is specified properly to use Ntrials.

Any insight on this would be much appreciated!
Thanks,
Romain

messages.body_plain:
Hi,

“factors” is one of the R problem children. ;)

With ~ 1 + myfactor, model.matrix can detect the redundancy in the model and by default eliminates a factor level. It could in theory do that with
~ -1 + intercept + myfactor
as well, if intercept was a covariate with all ones, but the more complex model definition setup in inla doesn’t try to guess as much as model.matrix what model you wanted to have.

Finn

messages.body_plain:
What’s the max.edge setting for the mesh? If the triangles are too large there will be bias in the parameter estimates.

With multiple likelihood’s and copy models, I would expect complex interaction of information flow between the models.

To check properly, you may need to run the estimation on simulated data, to see if it recovers the true parameters (or similar, since there is no guarantees in a single-realisation model...)

Finn

messages.body_plain:
Actually my specification of explicit intercept was a legacy from some old that I didn't think was needed to update - as I didn't exactly expect it to have aparticular effect.

It turns out that simplifying the intercept specification to

formula <- Y ~ 1 + TESTFAC

 works perfectly well in my case.

Thanks for the help!
Romain

So the estimated ranges are smaller than, or on the same order as, the triangle edges.
That should result in bias in the variance parameters estimates, so that might explain the results you see; the interpretation of the variance parameter simply doesn’t hold when the triangles are too large.  I believe we discussed/illustrated this a bit in the discussion part of the Lindgren et al 2011 JRSSB read paper on the link between SPDEs and GMRFs.

Finn

messages.subject: Optimization of binomial model with 4 million data (new to INLA)
messages.subject_clean: Optimization of binomial model with 4 million data (new to INLA)
messages.body_plain:
Dear group,
I'm totally new to INLA and I'm trying to run a binomial model with a large dataset of 4 million data. I got some help from a colleague to start with but still I'm a bit confused.
I'm investigating if the condition of an animal ("atrisk" is my response variable and gets "0" is the animal is in a safe area, and "1" if it is at a risky area) is dependent on a series of explanatory variables. I expect linear effects for some of them, and non-linear effects for two of them (included as rw2). I have many individuals measured that I need to include as random factors, and also strong temporal autocorrelation within each animal.
After reading some thread on the group I have tried the model below, in which all variables are scaled. I have defined the "diagonals" for the "rw2" terms as suggested in some other threads, and also the argument control.inla that you see  below.

inla_bin<- inla(atrisk ~ 1 + Lcm + distance_to_border+ areahr + PPscore+
                  f(week, model="rw2",cyclic=TRUE, diagonal=1e-4)+
                  f(hour,model="rw2",cyclic=TRUE,diagonal=1e-4)+
                  f(tag_id_inla,model="iid")+

messages.body_plain:
Hi Finn,

Thanks for going through this in such detail and writing this much more clearly. For this example, z is a property of an individual (specifically antibody titre levels) so the mixture model would be used to estimate whether an individual was infected or non-infected and used to estimate spatial patterns of infected individuals.

I'll take a look more at inlabru and see if I can think of how to simplify this model at all.

Thanks again

On Tuesday, 7 May 2019 20:54:51 UTC+1, Finn Lindgren wrote:

> Hi,
>

> let me write that in (hopefully) more precise mathematical notation,
> to make sure I understand what you mean.
> Some notation:
> - \phi, the density function of a standard N(0,1) variable.
> - z, a known (or measured) value for a specific individual
> - \pi, u_1, u_2, s_1, s_2, unknown parameters, to be estimated.
> - prob(z), the probability (or rather conditional probability) an
> identified individual is infection positive
>
> prob(z) = \pi \phi[(z-u_1) / s_1] / s_1 / \{ \pi \phi[(z-u_1) / s_1] /
> s_1 + (1-\pi) \phi[(z-u_2) / s_2] / s_2 \}
>
> There's a practical difference here if z is a property of the
> individual, or if it's a property of a _potential_ individual with
> certain characteristics.
> Example from ecology:
> - the size of a group of dolphins in a property of each specific group
> - the roughness of the sea is a property of the ocean in which the dolphins live
> Both affect detectability of groups. However, one cannot have group
> size without a group, but the state of the
> sea at a certain potential group location doesn't care if there is a
> group there or not.
>
> In the group size case one needs to model the distribution of group
> sizes (possibly with space dependent parameters) explicitly, since one
> needs to know what characteristics a specific group that was or
> _wasn't_ observed might have.
> In the sea state case, one just needs to extend the model into
> time-dependent detectability.
>
> I don't quite see how your problem would motivate using the above
> probability as a thinning probability for a Poisson process, or what
> "z" is, and what the domain of the point process would be. However,
> assuming that is what you need, in inlabru you could define a model
> with predictor
>   \eta(s,z) = \log \lambda(s) + \log prob(z)
>
> You would need \pi, u_!, u_2, and s_1, and s_2 to be defined as
> transformation of latent gaussian variables, e.g.
> \pi = inverselogit(w_1)
> u_1 = w_2
> u_2 = w_3
> s_1 = exp(w_4)
> s_2 = exp(w_5)
> where each w is a N(0,1) "iid" latent gaussian variable.
>
> The resulting nonlinear model in the w-parameters is linearised iteratively.
> In this case, the resulting prob(z) model doesn't look very appealing
> to estimate, as it will be hard to identify the parameters, so I'm not
> sure how practical this particular approach would be.
>
> Finn
>
>
>
>
>

IMHO you should also provide custom priors. 'Small' values (range 5 -10) can result in huge effects in combination with a logit link. https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/oik.05985 is a nice paper about this. Consider `rw1` instead of the `ar1`. It can model the same complexity with a single hyperparameter.

And check your data for quasicomplete separation.

messages.body_plain:
For your question: Yes, this is why I said "just to test". The point is not to look at the results, but at the computational time.

I would suggest strong shrinkage priors in any case! Binomial data can "run away" sometimes.

If you save your logfile (with verbose=T), we can take a quick look and see if the convergence is bad.

Some times, people code the group-thing not from 1 to 49 but from 1901 to 1949, so INLA believes it must represent 1949 replicates.

Haakon

messages.body_plain:
Hi,

That the predictions for the fitted values are computed from the linear predictor, meaning they are influenced by and random effects in the predictor, is as I suspected.

Because mine is an animal model, it includes generic0 random effects e.g. in the form of the A inverse. As these type of effects are not of the classical style then probably I cannot assume a mean of zero, hence these type of random effects may influence the predictions.

I would therefore like to compute the predictions using only the fixed effects by posterior sampling, however have been having a difficult time trying to achieve this over the past weeks. Could you possibly give a brief explanation of how to do this for an example model where x1 and x2 are continuous covariates, x3 is a factor with 3 levels, and f(animal) and f(year) are the two random effects that I do not want to influence the predictions for y:

y ~ x1 + x2 + x3 + f(year, model="iid"...) + f(animal, model="generic0, Cmatrix=Ainv...)

Best,
Sarah

> the predictions from the fitted values are computed from the linear

> included in the fitted values. Often, is the random effects are of the
> 'classical style', like model="iid", then their mean is zero so the
> predictions with and without the random effects will mostly differ in
> the variance (although E(exp(...))  depends also on the variance of
> ...).

> you want to, either by using posterior samples, as you mention, or
> using linear combinations (see the FAQ page).

> > the predictions must be computed on the latent scale. As comparison,
> > in an MCMCglmm model output the predict(model, type="terms") function
> > would allow me to get these values.
> >
> > Currently I have used "control.compute=list(dic=T,config = TRUE)"
> > when running my INLA models, and obtained the predicted values for my
> > original data (i.e. not including NAs in the response phenotype)

> > Sarah Lundregan

messages.subject: Random Walk Precision Matrix: what does INLA output?
messages.subject_clean: Random Walk Precision Matrix: what does INLA output?
messages.body_plain:
Hello,

I am trying to understand what quantity INLA outputs in the random-effects block of the precision matrix for a RW1 model. I have the following tiny example:

```r
n <- 5
set.seed(79687)
u <- runif(n) # Covariates to be modelled smoothly
eta <- cos(u) + rnorm(n,0,exp(-12))
y <- rnorm(n,eta,.1)

df <- tibble(y = y,u = u)

inlaiid <- inla(
  y ~ 1 + f(u,model = "iid",initial = 0,fixed = TRUE)
  data = df,
  family = "gaussian",
  control.family = list(initial = 0,fixed = TRUE),
  control.inla = list(strategy='gaussian',int.strategy = "eb",correct = FALSE),
  control.compute=list(config=TRUE),
  control.predictor = list(compute=TRUE,initial = 0,fixed = TRUE),
  control.fixed = list(prec.intercept = 0,mean.intercept = 0)
)

inla_Q <- forceSymmetric(inlaiid$misc$config$config[[1]]$Q,'U')
inla_Q
```

I am able to manually reproduce the contents of inla_Q for this IID model. I set all precisions to 1 (i.e. log-precisions to 0) just to make the output easier to read, I know this is not the proper way to approach this if this were a real problem.

When running the same thing for a RW1 model on the random effect, I notice two things that confuse me:
1) The "linear predictor" and "fixed effects" blocks of inla_Q are understandable to me (given the math I have worked out); the "random effects" block (indices 6 - 10 in my concrete example) contains numbers I completely can't reproduce, and
2) When I run the model with the default sum-to-zero constraint, and when I run it with the first coordinate constrained to be zero and no sum-to-zero constraint, I get the same inla_Q matrix.

II would really appreciate anyone helping to clear up: what quantity does misc$config$config[[1]]$Q contain in this situation? Is it the rank-deficient RW1 precision matrix, or the full-rank matrix obtained by applying the linear constraint? The output has full dimension and full rank, so I am pretty confused by this. I have read chapter 3 of Rue and Held (2005) and still don't understand.

Code for RW1:

```r
inlarw1 <- inla(
  y ~ 1 + f(u,model = "iid",initial = 0,fixed = TRUE),
  data = df,
  family = "gaussian",
  control.family = list(initial = 0,fixed = TRUE),
  control.inla = list(strategy='gaussian',int.strategy = "eb",correct = FALSE),
  control.compute=list(config=TRUE),
  control.predictor = list(compute=TRUE,initial = 0,fixed = TRUE),
  control.fixed = list(prec.intercept = 0,mean.intercept = 0)
)
```

Code for RW1 with manual constraint:

```r
# Constraints
constr_A <- matrix(c(1,rep(0,n-1)),nrow = 1)
constr_e <- rep(0,nrow(constr_A))

# Fit INLA
inlarw1constr <- inla(
  y ~ 1 + f(u,model = "iid",initial = 0,fixed = TRUE,constr = FALSE,extraconstr = list(A = constr_A,e = constr_e)),
  data = df,
  family = "gaussian",
  control.family = list(initial = 0,fixed = TRUE),
  control.inla = list(strategy='gaussian',int.strategy = "eb",correct = FALSE),
  control.compute=list(config=TRUE),
  control.predictor = list(compute=TRUE,initial = 0,fixed = TRUE),
  control.fixed = list(prec.intercept = 0,mean.intercept = 0)
)
```

Thank you in advance to anyone who takes the time to read this and offer advice!

Alex

messages.body_plain:
I have seen the post by Matt Tuson asking if is it possible to fit a model with a non-symmetric adjacency matrix.

I am trying to fit a BYM model for data of geographical areas that are very unevenly structured so I set the adjacency matrix for a knn (k=5). R-INLA seems to get stuck in multiple attempts to factorize the sparse-matrix and sends the message: "I will try to fix it". The model is eventually fitted.
When I run the same model using a Queen specification for the adjacency matrix, the model runs much more faster.

Although is expected that there would be differences in the regression coefficients for each specification, there are significant differences!
You can see the code and data to reproduce the models.

>From these issues, I have two questions:

1. Are the results of the model with the knn specification still valid? (from the discussion of Matt's posts I didn't get a clear answer that an INLA model with a non-symmetric adjacency matrix is still correct)
2. Are the very small coefficients found in a knn specification related to the asymmetry of the adjacency matrix?

I appreciate your help and comments,
Best,  Jack.

messages.body_plain:
Hi Jack,

and adjacency matrix doesn't define a Markov random field _by_itself_,
so whether a GMRF can be defined using an asymmetric adjacency matrix
depends on _how_ the matrix is intended to be used. Precision matrices
must be symmetric positive definite matrices, which places fundamental
theoretical restrictions on what can be done.

In the full conditional distribution specifications of the Besag model
(and where the Besag model appears in the BYM), certain symmetry
properties are required, since it's not the directed conditionals that
are specified, but the full conditionals. In the previous thread, I
believe we also discussed SAR models, which _can_ be defined via
directed graphs without other restrictions on the graph structure. See
the Besag 1974 JRSSB discussion paper and the Rue and Held 2005 book
on Gaussian Markov random fields for more details of how neighbourhood
properties work in graph based Markov models.

Finn

multivariate Normal, there is no such thing as non-symmetry.

If A is the non-symmetric adj matrix, I guess it will appear as AA^T,
in the prec/cov, hence its symmetric, so there exists a symmetric adj
matrix, B, say, so that AA^T = BB^T

INLA assumes a symmetric graph, and if you input a non-symmetric one,
it depends on how its coded, what it means, as it assumes its
symmetric.

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Can R-INLA fit a model using the knn algorythm ?
messages.subject_clean: [r-inla] Can R-INLA fit a model using the knn algorythm ?
messages.body_plain:
To link this to my answer; the AA' construction is what would appear
in a directed hierarchical tree model.
Once the joint distribution has been obtained, this can be rewritten
as a model on the undirected graph defined by the non-sparse pattern
of AA'.

The problem with using asymmetric A directly in the full conditional
distribution expressions (e.g. saying that the conditional expectation
should be a weighted average of the "upstream" neighbours") is that
this doesn't guarantee the existence of a valid joint model. The Besag
model full conditional can only look the way they do because they are
constructed in precisely such a way that they do generate a valid
joint model.  The clique potentials etc in the general MRF theory
relates directly to this, so this is a well known fundamental property
of any and all Markov random field models.

Finn

messages.subject_clean: [r-inla] How to fit slm model with the error term not follow iid distribution？
messages.body_plain:
I would suggest trying:
1. Fix the likelihood noise to be very small, e.g. logprecision = 8
2. Use generic0 to add your noise as a random effect to the model
3. When reporting the linear predictor, manually sample from the not-noise components and compute what you need

PS: Your product structure may make this impossible, depending on details. My tip is general for "I want correlated noise in my model"

Best,
Haakon

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Random Walk Precision Matrix: what does INLA output?
messages.subject_clean: [r-inla] Random Walk Precision Matrix: what does INLA output?
messages.body_plain:
Thanks! Those calculations match what I have so that's very encouraging. What I am confused about are the dimension and rank of A and Q for a random walk 1. If your f_1 term has a RW1 model, then m1 = n, but my understanding is that rank(A) = rank(Q) = n-1, and one linear constraint is needed. From the GMRF book, I understand that computations can proceed using such a singular precision matrix, with determinants being taken as the product of only the non-zero eigenvalues etc, and then (as you say) the mean and variance are corrected at the end only, using available formulas.

This would all make sense to me, but when I run the RW1 model as initially posted, with inla_Q as the output of misc$config$config[[1]]$Q, I get
> dim(inla_Q)
[1] 11 11
> rankMatrix(inla_Q)
[1] 11

n = 5 so this dimension corresponds to 5 nodes in the latent field, 5 random effects (random walk evaluations), and the intercept, which makes sense. But why is it full rank? Does INLA do something here that is documented elsewhere, or am I misunderstanding the basic theory? My understanding of your previous response is that this should actually be rank 10.

Really appreciate you taking the time!

Alex

On Wednesday, May 15, 2019 at 1:47:56 AM UTC-4, Helpdesk wrote:

> Hi,
>
> these computations are spelled out here
>
> Article{art632,
>   author =       {H. Rue and A. Riebler and S. H. S{\o}rbye and J. B.
>                   Illian and D. P. Simpson and F. K. Lindgren},
>   title =        {Bayesian Computing with {INLA}: {A} Review},
>   journal =      {Annual Reviews of Statistics and Its Applications},
>   keywords =     {year2017,my.own,my.cv <http://my.cv>},
>   year =         2017,
>   volume =       4,
>   number =       {March},
>   pages =        {395--421},
>   doi =          {10.1146/annurev-statistics-060116-054045}
> }
>
> or check the arxiv version.
>
> The constraints are not part of the precision matrix, as they are used
> to correct the mean/variance, as describer in the GMRF book section
> 2.3.3
>
>
> If its still unclear, let me know
>
> H
>
>
>
>
> On Tue, 2019-05-14 at 13:47 -0700, Alex Stringer wrote:
> > Hello,
> >
> > I am trying to understand what quantity INLA outputs in the random-
> > effects block of the precision matrix for a RW1 model. I have the
> > following tiny example:
> >
> > ```r
> > n <- 5
> > set.seed(79687)
> > u <- runif(n) # Covariates to be modelled smoothly
> > eta <- cos(u) + rnorm(n,0,exp(-12))
> > y <- rnorm(n,eta,.1)
> >
> > df <- tibble(y = y,u = u)
> >
> > inlaiid <- inla(
> >   y ~ 1 + f(u,model = "iid",initial = 0,fixed = TRUE)
> >   data = df,
> >   family = "gaussian",
> >   control.family = list(initial = 0,fixed = TRUE),
> >   control.inla = list(strategy='gaussian',int.strategy = "eb",correct
> > = FALSE),
> >   control.compute=list(config=TRUE),
> >   control.predictor = list(compute=TRUE,initial = 0,fixed = TRUE),
> >   control.fixed = list(prec.intercept = 0,mean.intercept = 0)
> > )
> >
> > inla_Q <- forceSymmetric(inlaiid$misc$config$config[[1]]$Q,'U')
> > inla_Q
> > ```
> >
> > I am able to manually reproduce the contents of inla_Q for this IID
> > model. I set all precisions to 1 (i.e. log-precisions to 0) just to
> > make the output easier to read, I know this is not the proper way to
> > approach this if this were a real problem.
> >
> > When running the same thing for a RW1 model on the random effect, I
> > notice two things that confuse me:
> > 1) The "linear predictor" and "fixed effects" blocks of inla_Q are
> > understandable to me (given the math I have worked out); the "random
> > effects" block (indices 6 - 10 in my concrete example) contains
> > numbers I completely can't reproduce, and
> > 2) When I run the model with the default sum-to-zero constraint, and
> > when I run it with the first coordinate constrained to be zero and no
> > sum-to-zero constraint, I get the same inla_Q matrix.
> >
> > II would really appreciate anyone helping to clear up: what quantity
> > does misc$config$config[[1]]$Q contain in this situation? Is it the
> > rank-deficient RW1 precision matrix, or the full-rank matrix obtained
> > by applying the linear constraint? The output has full dimension and
> > full rank, so I am pretty confused by this. I have read chapter 3 of
> > Rue and Held (2005) and still don't understand.
> >
> > Code for RW1:
> >
> > ```r
> > inlarw1 <- inla(
> >   y ~ 1 + f(u,model = "iid",initial = 0,fixed = TRUE),
> >   data = df,
> >   family = "gaussian",
> >   control.family = list(initial = 0,fixed = TRUE),
> >   control.inla = list(strategy='gaussian',int.strategy = "eb",correct
> > = FALSE),
> >   control.compute=list(config=TRUE),
> >   control.predictor = list(compute=TRUE,initial = 0,fixed = TRUE),
> >   control.fixed = list(prec.intercept = 0,mean.intercept = 0)
> > )
> > ```
> >
> > Code for RW1 with manual constraint:
> >
> > ```r
> > # Constraints
> > constr_A <- matrix(c(1,rep(0,n-1)),nrow = 1)
> > constr_e <- rep(0,nrow(constr_A))
> >
> > # Fit INLA
> > inlarw1constr <- inla(
> >   y ~ 1 + f(u,model = "iid",initial = 0,fixed = TRUE,constr =
> > FALSE,extraconstr = list(A = constr_A,e = constr_e)),
> >   data = df,
> >   family = "gaussian",
> >   control.family = list(initial = 0,fixed = TRUE),
> >   control.inla = list(strategy='gaussian',int.strategy = "eb",correct
> > = FALSE),
> >   control.compute=list(config=TRUE),
> >   control.predictor = list(compute=TRUE,initial = 0,fixed = TRUE),
> >   control.fixed = list(prec.intercept = 0,mean.intercept = 0)
> > )
> > ```
> >
> > Thank you in advance to anyone who takes the time to read this and
> > offer advice!
> >
> > Alex

Does INLA do proportional hazards models? The likelihood for each data point depends on more than one node in the latent field. My understanding was that INLA fits survival models by directly estimating the hazard function, and hence these types of models which have likelihoods which are of the same functional form as a Cox PH partial likelihood can't be fit using the INLA software using the same tricks used by survival::clogit, mgcv::gam, and so on.

Alex

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Can R-INLA fit a model using the knn algorythm ?
messages.subject_clean: [r-inla] Can R-INLA fit a model using the knn algorythm ?
messages.body_plain:
Hi Havard and Finn,
Thanks for your replies.

Following on Havard's comment "INLA assumes a symmetric graph, and if you input a non-symmetric one, it depends on how its coded, what it means, as it assumes its symmetric"; I don't see any issue with the specification of the Adjacency Matrix (AM) in my code:

> temp <- knn2nb(knearneigh(map, k=5, RANN = FALSE))
> nb2INLA("LDN.graph",temp)
> LDN.adj <- paste(getwd(),"/LDN.graph",sep="")

The model is then specified as:

> formula <- y ~ 1 + f(ID, model="bym", graph=LDN.adj) + x1+x2+x3
> mod <- inla(formula,family="poisson",data=data,E=Expected, control.predictor=list(compute=TRUE), control.compute=list(dic=TRUE,cpo=TRUE))

If an asymmetric AM doesn't allow generating a valid joint model (Finn's comment),  would it be ok without including covariates x1, x2 and x3 in the model?

On the other hand, Do the estimation of very small coefficients have to do with the asymmetry of the AM. The regression coefficients from the model are: x1=0.0000; x2=0.0001; x3=-0.0004. If I use a queen specification for the AM or even if I make the AM symmetric (with the make.nb.sym function), the coefficients change significantly ( x1=-0.011; x2=0.0003; x3=0.0041 ).

with the asymmetric AM, R-INLA sends the message "I will try to fix it". Does R-INLA select a subset of neighbors that have symmetry? Or are the small coefficients related to priors specified for the fixed component and the sampler gets stuck in a narrow range of values and is not able to  explore the posterior distribution correctly?

Thanks in advance,
Jack,

> multivariate Normal, there is no such thing as non-symmetry.

> If A is the non-symmetric adj matrix, I guess it will appear as AA^T,
> in the prec/cov, hence its symmetric, so there exists a symmetric adj
> matrix, B, say, so that AA^T = BB^T
>
> INLA assumes a symmetric graph, and if you input a non-symmetric one,

>
> H

messages.subject_clean: Invalid links for SPDE-tutorial
messages.body_plain:
Hi everyone,

I'm a very very beginner in this world of analysis and am in the process of learning INLA for my thesis (I know, it's quite the challenge). I've been making use of the tutorial found here: http://www.r-inla.org/examples/tutorials/spde-tutorial. However, none of the links to the datasets for the sample problems seem to be working.

For example, here's one for section 2.1:
http://www.math.ntnu.no/inla/r-inla.org/ tutorials/spde/R/spde-tutorial-rain.R

Does anyone know where I can find the correct links or datasets for this tutorial?

Thanks!

> Hi Havard and Finn,

>
> Following on Havard's comment "INLA assumes a symmetric graph, and if

> > nb2INLA("LDN.graph",temp)

Hi,

what I ment, is for the bym model, the 'graph' is assumed to be
symmetric. seen from a matrix point of view, only the upper part of it,
or the lower part of it, has to be read. which one it is, depends on
the coding. so, if you input a non-symmetric one, then you have to read
the code to figure out what is actually happening.

no, this has nothing to do with the covariates x1..x3.

> On the other hand, Do the estimation of very small coefficients have

you can try. if the graph is non-symmetric, do

A = inla.graph2matrix(inla.read.graph(LDN.adj))

to make it symmetric (using the 'union')

it can be a bi-effect of this, try the above trick to check.

messages.subject: Two stage latent model (not sure what else to call it)
messages.subject_clean: Two stage latent model (not sure what else to call it)
messages.body_plain:
Hello,

I'm trying to figure out if INLA can help me model something involving two "stages".

As an illustrative example:

We'll model the probability of a student getting accepted to university as a basic logistic regression with 4-5 covariates.

One of those covariates is their SAT score.

The SAT score is log-normally distributed and depends on 3-4 additional covariates (different than what is in the logistic model.)

In rough math:

P(Accept) ~ 1/(1+exp(-eta))
eta = cov_1 * beta_1 + cov_2 * beta_2 + SAT * beta_3
SAT ~ N(mu, sigma)
mu = cov_4 * beta_4 + cov_5 * beta_5 + cov_6 * beta_6

The idea is that for a student who doesn't have an SAT score yet, we will sample possible scores from the posterior of the log-normal model, then use those samples as input to the logistic regression, where will again sample from the posterior of the logistic regression model. In layman's terms "The uncertainty of the SAT score will carry through and influence the uncertainty of the logistic model"

Is modeling something like this possible in INLA?

Thanks!!

Many thanks in advance.

Hi Finn,

The model is a Poisson model (number of GP visits per person), a and b are variables at the individual level (coded as 0 and 1), c and d are variables at the aggregated level (e.g. GPs per 100.000 persons). Additionally, I used a besag prior to account for spatial proximity.

this is the code I used.

model <- inla(GP_contacts~  1 + a+ b+ c+ d+
                           f(idx.alter, AGE, model = "rw2", scale.model = T, hyper = list(theta = list(prior="pc.prec", param=c(1,0.001)))) +
                             f(idx1, model = "besag",
                               graph = "D:/INLA/Gyn", scale.model = T, hyper = list(theta = list(prior="pc.prec", param=c(1,0.001)))),
                           family = "poisson", data=Gesamt, control.compute = list(dic=T, openmp.strategy = "huge"),
                           control.inla = list(strategy = "gaussian", int.strategy = "eb", reordering = "amdc"), verbose = T)

summary(model)
>

messages.body_plain:
OK,
then the rw2 component can be (mostly) interpreted as the age effect
that is not explained by the combination of the other components. If
any of the other components, such as a,b,c, and d also vary with age,
then the rw2 component by itself doesn't give the absolute relative
risk per age. The peak at 17 therefore needs to be set in relation to
what the rest of the model says. For example, it might be picking up
some nonlinear effect that the linear covariate models can't
represent.
But perhaps more importantly, you really need to include the posterior
uncertainty when plotting the results before drawing too strong
conclusions.

Finn

On Wed, 22 May 2019 at 12:52, 'Boris' via R-inla discussion group
<r-inla-disc...@googlegroups.com> wrote:
> I do understand that the coefficients are to be interpreted in relation to what the rest of the model says. However, I would like to know what the precise communication of the results of the rw2 model then is.
>
> Is the precise wording e.g. "persons aged 17 years have a 1.22 higher risk than all other age groups after accounting for a,b,c and d"

No, that can't be right, since all age groups above 10 have odds ratio
above 1; the 17 year olds just have higher than the others, not 1.22
higher! E.g., for age group 20 it's close to 1.2, so nearly the same
as for 17.
The graph label says "odds ratio", but you're talking about the rw2
component; I'm not sure how you get the former from the latter. You
may need to be more specific in how you define that odds ratio, so
that there is no doubt about what the risk is elevated in relation
_to_; unfortunately I haven't worked with that kind of model, so can't
give very specific advice on that point.
I suspect that "persons aged 17 years have a 22% higher risk than
explained by the covariates alone" (or "the rest of the model") is a
valid statement, but to compare the age groups with each other, I
suspect you need to do that more explicitly.

> Also, the uncertainty is plotted in the graph - thanks for the hint. However, as this is a dataset with 800.000 individuals, the uncertainty is quite small.

Ahhh, yes, I see the tiny grey bands now!

Finn

messages.body_plain:
Dear all,

I'm using a negative binomial model with f(LocationID, model = "iid", constr = TRUE, hyper = list(theta = list(prior = "pc.prec", param = c(1, 1e-9)))). The estimated median precision of this random effect is 0.39, which is much too small given the prior. Changing the alpha parameter of the prior has no impact on the posterior. What is going on here?

There are about 800 locations, each with about 100 observations. The top 10 random effects have a mean ranging from 3.6 to 4.7. The associated observations range from 6 to 516 (5%/95% quantile). The top 10 lowest random effects have a mean ranging from -3.7 to -3.3. The associated observations range from 0 to 1. Only 4 non-zero observations per locations.

Best regards,

Thierry

function (prec, u, alpha, lambda, log = FALSE)
{
    lambda = inla.pc.prec.lambda(u, alpha, lambda)
    s = 1/sqrt(prec)
    d = dexp(s, rate = lambda, log = log)
    log.jac = -log(2) - 3/2 * log(prec)
    if (log) {
        return(d + log.jac)
    }
    else {
        return(d * exp(log.jac))
    }

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Can R-INLA fit a model using the knn algorythm ?
messages.subject_clean: [r-inla] Can R-INLA fit a model using the knn algorythm ?
messages.body_plain:
Hi Havard,
Thanks for your reply and suggestions.
I tried building the AM as you suggested and in fact it fitted the model without any issues, yet the value and direction of the regression coefficients were different (which I wasn't expecting).
I couldn't verify the structure of the adjacency matrix from the "g = inla.read.graph(A + t(A))" instruction but I run another model with an adjacency matrix forced to be symmetric (using the spdep package, before converting the AM to an LDN.adj) and as I expected, the results of this other model were identical to the ones with the "g = inla.read.graph(A + t(A))" instruction.

In brief; while the suggested "union" of the AM worked in terms of running a "smooth / faster" inla model, the model did not incorporate the KNN spatial structure I wanted. In the KNN model each area has 5 neighbors while the symmetric AM (whether from a previous symmetric AM or after adjusting it with the union) has 6.2 neighbors in average.

I explored the messages sent (using the verbose=TRUE) and it looks like R-inla does some kind of approximation to fit the model with the asymmetric AM, but I couln't (also don't know how to) verify that's the case. I looked for the message "I will try to fix it" from sending inla() in the console but I couldn't find it either. Do you know what is the procedure the program follows for the "I will try to fix it".

I am sorry to keep asking these questions but in my case is imperative to use a KNN spatial structure.

Thanks in advance,

Jack

On Monday, 20 May 2019 13:59:38 UTC+10, Helpdesk wrote:

> > Hi Havard and Finn,
> > Thanks for your replies.
> >
> > Following on Havard's comment "INLA assumes a symmetric graph, and if
> > you input a non-symmetric one, it depends on how its coded, what it
> > means, as it assumes its symmetric"; I don't see any issue with the
> > specification of the Adjacency Matrix (AM) in my code:
> >
> > > temp <- knn2nb(knearneigh(map, k=5, RANN = FALSE))
> > > nb2INLA("LDN.graph",temp)
> > > LDN.adj <- paste(getwd(),"/LDN.graph",sep="")
>
>
> Hi,
>
> what I ment, is for the bym model, the 'graph' is assumed to be
> symmetric. seen from a matrix point of view, only the upper part of it,
> or the lower part of it, has to be read. which one it is, depends on
> the coding. so, if you input a non-symmetric one, then you have to read
> the code to figure out what is actually happening.
>
> > The model is then specified as:
> >
> > > formula <- y ~ 1 + f(ID, model="bym", graph=LDN.adj) + x1+x2+x3
> > > mod <- inla(formula,family="poisson",data=data,E=Expected,
> > control.predictor=list(compute=TRUE),
> > control.compute=list(dic=TRUE,cpo=TRUE))
> >
> > If an asymmetric AM doesn't allow generating a valid joint model
> > (Finn's comment),  would it be ok without including covariates x1, x2
> > and x3 in the model?
>
> no, this has nothing to do with the covariates x1..x3.
>
> > On the other hand, Do the estimation of very small coefficients have
> > to do with the asymmetry of the AM.
>
> you can try. if the graph is non-symmetric, do
>
> A = inla.graph2matrix(inla.read.graph(LDN.adj))
> g = inla.read.graph(A + t(A))
>
> to make it symmetric (using the 'union')
>
>
>
>
> > with the asymmetric AM, R-INLA sends the message "I will try to fix
> > it".
>
> it can be a bi-effect of this, try the above trick to check.
> --
> Håvard Rue

messages.body_plain:
Hi & thanks for your email.

Using knn to define neighbours do not give symmetry, like i could be a
neigb of j, but not the oposite. The input to some of the models
requiring a graph, assumes the graph to be symmetric. How you want to
symmetrice it, its up to you but using

A+t(A)

is the union, if i~j, then we must have j~i.

The Gaussian distribution is 'symmetric' in this sense, Cor(x_i, x_j) =
Cor(x_j, x_i)  and there is no way around this.

Best
H

messages.subject: Bayesian spatial modelling with INLA using two different likelihoods of data with unequal sample size
messages.subject_clean: Bayesian spatial modelling with INLA using two different likelihoods of data with unequal sample size
messages.body_plain:
Hi Dear INLA users,

I have some questions about the Bayesian modeling based on INLA using multiple likelihoods.

When reading the following two papers:

- Martins TG, Simpson D, Lindgren F, Rue H (2013) Bayesian computing with INLA: New features. Computational Statistics & Data Analysis 67:68–83. doi: 10.1016/j.csda.2013.04.014 <https://doi.org/10.1016/j.csda.2013.04.014>

- Illian JB, Martino S, Sørbye SH, et al (2013) Fitting complex ecological point process models with integrated nested Laplace approximation. Methods in Ecology and Evolution 4:305–315. doi: 10.1111/2041-21...@10.1111/(ISSN)2041-210X.STATSTOO, <https://doi.org/10.1111/204...@10.1111/(ISSN)2041-210X.STATSTOO>

I found out that it is possible to fit Bayesian models with INLA using multiple likelihoods. For all the cas studies above, the sample sizes of the data implying the two likelihoods are equal.
A typical example in forestry is the marked point process models (see Illian et al. 2013), where in addition to the observed individuals (i.e. spatial locations of a species, which is modelled by point process likelihood), we have additional information related to the health status of each species (modeled by binomial likelihood) or the diameter of each species (which can be modeled by Gaussian likelihood).

However, let's suppose that, the data available for the second likelihood is aggregated in grid cells (e.g. a regular lattice), such that its sample size (say m) is less than the one of the first data (say n), of which individuals are observed at each spatial location. As example, see the Dorazio's approach proposed in Species Distribution Models (Dorazio RM (2014) Accounting for imperfect detection and survey bias in statistical analysis of presence‐only data. Global Ecology and Biogeography 23:1472–1484. doi: 10.1111/geb.12216) <https://doi.org/10.1111/geb.12216> , which includes two likelihoods: Poisson point process likelihood for the presence-only data and Poisson likelihood for the point-counts (aggregated data in grid cells).
